chunks: From him, from Safwan and Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who pays in advance (salam) twenty dinars for a sale of grain or dates, and lends the owner of the salam ten or twenty dinars. He (the Imam) said: 'It is not valid if the loan is one that entails a benefit (qarḍan yajurru shay'an), so it is not valid.'

And I asked him about a man who goes to his partner (harīf) and companion (khalīṭ) to borrow dinars, and he lends them to him; if it were not for the fact that he associates with him, partners with him, and gains profit from him, he would not lend to him. He (the Imam) said: 'If it is well-known between them [that the loan is for partnership purposes], there is no objection; but if he only lends him because he gains profit from him, then it is not valid.'

key_terms.حَرِيف: Partner in a business or property
key_terms.خَلِيط: Companion or close associate in trade
key_terms.سَلَمَ: To pay in advance for goods to be delivered later (Salam contract)
key_terms.قَرْضاً يَجُرُّ شَيْئاً: A loan that entails/leads to a benefit (interest-like feature)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a loan given to a business partner to facilitate profit-sharing?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between a pure loan and one given as a means to secure commercial advantage, ruling that if the loan is contingent upon benefiting from the partnership (salām or harif), it is invalid due to the hidden interest (riba). This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the intention and causal link between the loan and the subsequent gain, ensuring the transaction remains a benevolent act rather than a disguised trade. The exception for well-established relationships underscores the flexibility in recognizing customary business practices when the loan is not merely a pretext for profit.
